strengths: Comprehensive unified framework: MotionLLaMA is the first motion-centric multimodal LLM (to my knowledge) that jointly handles both single-person and dual-person motion synthesis and comprehension within a single autoregressive paradigm, covering 9 tasks (T2M, M2T, M2D, D2M, S2G, IT2M, IM2T, motion in-between, motion completion), as summarized in Table 1. This breadth is a genuine advance over prior motion LLMs (MotionGPT, LMM, MoGPT, MotionAgent) that cover fewer tasks.

The HoMi Tokenizer is a well-motivated technical contribution: separate encoders for hand vs. torso address a real problem (hand motion has distinct amplitude/frequency statistics), and the bidirectional FFT + frequency-aware gating mechanism is a sensible way to capture temporal and cross-channel frequency structure. Table 5 shows that a single-codebook HoMi matches a six-codebook RVQ (MPJPE all 0.0526 vs 0.0529) and beats other single-codebook baselines, and Table 9 isolates the contributions of STH and FAMG.

Strong empirical validation: results on comprehension (Table 2), dual-person interaction (Table 3 lower), motion prediction/in-between (Table 4), dance-to-music (Table 7), and reconstruction (Table 5) are consistently at or near the top, with well-chosen metrics (R-Precision, MM-Dist, FID, FDE, BCS/BHS/F1, FGD/BA).

MotionHub is a substantial community resource: ~131k single-person motion clips with 270k captions, 21k dual-person clips with 63k captions, ~70 hours of motion data with audio, spanning 11 source datasets, with a documented standardization pipeline (unified coordinate system, motion retargeting, manual filtering, LLM-assisted re-annotation).

The paper is generally well-written, with clear motivation, a clean pipeline figure (Fig. 2), a helpful comparison table (Table 1), and thoughtful supplementary material (Sec. C on representation choice and codebook-size analysis, Table 11/12).
weaknesses: Overclaiming relative to evidence: the abstract states performance 'comparable to SOTA in the remaining tasks,' but Table 8 (Speech-to-Gesture) shows MotionLLaMA FGD 194.68 vs. MCM 146.01 and BA 0.2167 vs. MCM 0.2584, i.e., clearly below the strongest baseline on both quality and alignment metrics. Similarly, single-person T2M in Table 3 is below MoMask/MCM on R-Precision Top-1. The text should qualify these gaps rather than describe them as comparable.

Technical novelty of the LLM integration is limited: the tokenizer-autoregressive paradigm, modality-specific start/end tokens, LoRA fine-tuning of LLaMA, and the two-stage (unconditional pretrain + instruction tuning) recipe closely follow MotionGPT / LMM / MoGPT. The main novel element (HoMi tokenizer) is itself an incremental combination of existing ideas (VQ-VAE, FFT gating, disentangled encoders); the paper would be strengthened by ablating which component drives the gain over a strong single-codebook baseline rather than only against weaker ones.

MotionHub is largely a consolidation and re-annotation of 11 existing datasets rather than a new collection. The claim of being 'the most exhaustive multi-task human motion dataset' is plausible but not directly supported by a quantitative comparison table against other multi-task motion datasets. The use of ChatGPT-4o to rewrite/standardize captions also raises questions about annotation quality that are not analyzed.

Evidence for the single-codebook advantage is somewhat thin: the codebook-size selection is based on a single usage histogram (Fig. 4) and a single hyperparameter sweep (Table 12), and the RVQ comparison is a single number (Table 5). The claim that 'reconstruction accuracy with multiple codebooks does not necessarily equate to superior motion quality' is asserted rather than demonstrated with generative metrics.

Some design choices lack justification: the two-model variant (expert vs. unified) is mentioned but its evaluation is not clearly reported, and it is unclear whether the unified model is strictly worse on individual tasks. The temperature/top-p settings (0.6 / 0.9) and the 500-epoch training schedule are not ablated.

Limited discussion of failure cases and societal considerations (e.g., misuse of motion generation, licensing of source datasets redistributed in MotionHub). For a dataset contribution, licensing and consent details are typically expected.

strengths: Unified framework covering an unusually broad set of motion tasks (9 tasks: 6 synthesis, 3 comprehension) within a single LLaMA-3.2-based autoregressive model with LoRA fine-tuning, as summarized in Table 1 and demonstrated by the pipeline in Fig. 2.

The HoMi Tokenizer is a meaningful technical contribution: a single-codebook VQ-VAE that uses separate body/hand encoders (STH) and bidirectional FFT-based Frequency-Aware Motion Gating (FAMG) to reach reconstruction quality (Table 5) close to RVQ with six codebooks, while avoiding the sampling complexity of residual quantization. The ablation in Table 9 isolates the benefit of both components, and Table 12 justifies the codebook size choice empirically.

MotionHub is a substantial and useful resource: 131,515 single-person motion entries with 269,880 captions and 21,021 dual-person entries with 62,791 captions (~70 hours), consolidated from many public datasets with an explicit standardization/re-annotation pipeline (Table 10, Sec. A). This directly addresses the data-insufficiency problem for LLM-scale motion modeling, and the data is stated to be publicly released.

Broad, multi-task empirical validation with appropriate per-task metrics (FID, MM-Dist, R-Precision, BLEU/ROUGE/CIDEr/BERTScore, FGD/BA/L1Div, BCS/BHS/F1, MPJPE/ADE/FDE). Strong and consistent gains are reported for motion-to-text (Table 2), dance-to-music (Table 7), and motion completion/in-between (Table 4), with competitive T2M results (Table 3).

Good analytic depth beyond headline numbers: motion-representation study (Table 11) motivating global joint coordinates over translation/rotation or InterHuman-style representations, codebook utilization analysis (Fig. 4), and qualitative visualizations across tasks (Figs. 1, 5, 6).
The paper is clearly written, well organized, and the contribution list matches the presented evidence; code and dataset are said to be released, aiding reproducibility.
weaknesses: Some state-of-the-art claims in the abstract are not fully supported by the tables. For interaction dual-person text-to-motion the abstract claims SOTA, but Table 3 (lower) shows MotionLLaMA has markedly worse FID than InterGen (0.1133 vs. 0.0537) and worse than ComMDM/InterGen on Diversity (20.3434 vs. 20.6620). Similarly, the M2D results (Table 6) are only 'comparable' with a higher FID_k than some baselines, and the S2G FGD (194.68, Table 8) is worse than MCM (146.01). The claims should be tempered to match the evidence.

Technical novelty is largely integrative: the system combines a pre-trained LLaMA-3.2, LoRA, WavTokenizer, and a VQ-VAE with FFT gating. The genuinely new component (HoMi) is an incremental architectural modification, so the main contribution is engineering/comprehensive evaluation rather than a new methodological principle.

The dataset construction relies heavily on ChatGPT-4o for rewriting descriptions, generating captions for labeled data, and decomposing dual-person into single-person descriptions. The paper does not quantify how much of the annotation is model-generated, nor does it report human verification rates or inter-annotator agreement for these steps, raising concerns about annotation noise, stylistic bias, and evaluation circularity.

Evaluation of motion-to-text (Table 2) uses a TMR model trained on MotionHub itself to compute R-Precision and MM-Dist. While the 'Real' rows provide some anchoring, this introduces a potential favorable bias toward the proposed model's own data distribution and is not discussed as a limitation.

Limited evidence on data efficiency and scale claims: the paper motivates MotionHub by the need for large-scale data to fine-tune an LLaMA-level model, but provides no ablation on dataset size or on how much the re-annotation pipeline actually helps versus raw public datasets. Compute/training cost (500 epochs on all tasks) is not reported, which hinders reproducibility assessment.

The comparison in Table 1 is qualitative checkmarks only and may overstate coverage (e.g., several baselines are marked as not supporting tasks they arguably handle in limited form). No quantitative per-task baselines are given for some tasks (e.g., IM2T/IT2M comparisons are only partially supported).

No user study or perceptual evaluation is provided for the generation tasks, and failure cases are not analyzed; the limitations of the unified single-model approach (e.g., task interference between 9 tasks, which motivated separate 'expert' and 'unified' models in Sec. 4.1) are noted but not quantified.

strengths: Broad, genuinely useful task scope: a single autoregressive motion LLM covering 9 motion-centric tasks (T2M, M2T, music/dance both directions, S2G, IT2M, IM2T, motion completion, in-betweening) within one shared token vocabulary for text/motion/audio, including comparatively under-explored dual-person interaction generation. Table 1's multitask coverage is a real differentiator versus MotionGPT/MotionAgent/M³GPT/UniMuMo.

The HoMi tokenizer is a reasonable, practically motivated design (single 2048-entry codebook, disentangled hand/torso encoders, FFT-based frequency-aware gating), and the ablations support it: Table 9 shows a clear drop when STH/FAMG are removed (0.0526 -> 0.0695 MPJPE), Table 12 justifies the codebook size, and Table 5 shows a large gain over the vanilla VQ baseline (0.0842 -> 0.0526 MPJPE) while reaching RVQ-level accuracy with one codebook instead of six, which simplifies sampling.

MotionHub is a non-trivial curation effort: 11 public datasets consolidated with a unified coordinate system, retargeting, manual quality filtering, LLM-assisted re-annotation and text normalization, yielding ~131K single-person and ~21K dual-person clips with paired captions; dual-person interaction data with per-person descriptions remains scarce, so the aggregation has community value.

Evaluation breadth: each task is compared against task-specific baselines (TM2T, MotionGPT, MDM, MoMask, MCM, ComMDM, InterGen, M³GPT, FACT, Bailando, EDGE, CaMN, DiffStyleGesture) with standard metrics, plus tokenizer ablations and supplementary studies on motion representation (Table 11) and codebook size (Table 12).

Reasonable reporting of the training recipe (two-stage unconditional pretraining + instruction tuning, LoRA rank/alpha/dropout, LR, inference temperature/top-p, prompt-template count) and a promise of released code and dataset, which aids reproducibility.
weaknesses: Claims materially exceed the evidence. The abstract/introduction assert SOTA on motion completion, interaction T2M and 'all comprehension tasks' and 'comparable to SOTA' elsewhere, yet Table 3 shows T2M trailing MoMask/MCM on R-Precision (0.3389 vs 0.3654) and FID (0.0268 vs 0.0179), and Table 6 describes a music-to-dance FID_k of 58.56 vs M³GPT's 24.34 as 'slightly higher' (a 2.4x gap). Similarly, dual-person T2M is claimed SOTA while FID is >2x worse than InterGen (0.1133 vs 0.0537), with the claim resting on R-Precision alone. This selective framing is a substantive problem, not a wording nit.

Table 7 reports BCS 100.0 / BHS 97.0 / F1 98.5 on dance-to-music, which strongly suggests a saturated metric rather than genuine superiority; the 'Real' reference row is omitted for this table, so there is no sanity check that the metric can discriminate at all. This undermines the strongest-looking result in the paper.

Limited technical novelty relative to prior motion LLMs. The system composes existing parts (LLaMA-3.2-Instruct + LoRA, WavTokenizer, a VQ-VAE motion tokenizer with modest additions), and the pipeline mirrors MotionGPT/MotionAgent/M³GPT/UniMuMo. There is no new objective or architectural insight, and the paper does not clearly delimit what is new versus borrowed (e.g., the 'frequency-aware gating' is described only in one paragraph).

Baselines are inadequate for the tasks where SOTA is claimed. Motion completion/in-betweening (Table 4) is compared only to MDM and MotionGPT, neither designed for completion, and ADE/FDE are missing ('-') for the baselines, so no fair comparison is possible; dedicated completion/in-betweening methods (e.g., PriorMDM-style, double-take, DNO/HumanMAC) are absent. Speech-to-gesture omits full-body methods (e.g., EMAGE/HumanTomato) despite the fine-grained full-body claim, and music-to-dance omits diffusion-based dance generators.

The central 'unified vs. expert' argument is never evidenced: the paper states that both an expert and a unified model were trained, but no comparison (per-task degradation, task interference, or negative transfer) is reported anywhere in the main paper or supplement.

Tokenizer evidence is thin for the strength of the claims. Table 5's advantage over RVQ is marginal overall (0.0526 vs 0.0529 MPJPE) and actually worse on hands (0.0568 vs 0.0563), yet the tokenizer is framed as resolving the accuracy/efficiency trade-off. No statistical significance, per-dataset breakdown, or held-out codebook selection is provided (Table 12 selects the codebook on the same MotionHub data used for evaluation).

Dataset contribution has unresolved quality, licensing and ethics questions. Captions are rewritten by ChatGPT-4o with no reported human verification or accuracy audit; no discussion of consent, licensing, or privacy for aggregated human motion data; no clip-length/frame-count distributions, despite the 'most extensive' claim (70.10 hours is modest). The claim that MotionHub is the largest multi-task motion dataset is asserted rather than quantified against alternatives.

Missing methodological and analytical detail in the main text: no loss functions, no tokenizer training specifics (codebook initialization, commitment loss, downsample-rate justification), no model parameter counts or compute budget, no inference-cost comparison against baselines, no failure cases, and no limitations or societal-impact discussion despite working with human motion (deepfake/biometric misuse considerations).

Evaluation protocol concerns: R-Precision is computed with 256 samples per batch (Table 3 note), which is not the standard protocol used by the baselines, and the feature extractors for FID/MM-Dist are unspecified. The interaction-task metrics are adapted from single-person TMR without validation, and diversity/alignment trade-offs are not analyzed, so several 'SOTA' claims are not comparable across rows.

Presentation issues: Table 4's gray 'in-between' rows duplicate values ambiguously with missing baseline entries; supplementary sections are referenced as 'Sec A/B' from the main text; Table 1's checkmarks for prior methods are not justified with evidence; and several contributions (MotionHub size, 70.10 hours) are stated inconsistently with the supplementary statistics.
